title: The present tense, regular and irregular

tips.title: Chop the ending, add the new one
tips.body: For a regular verb: take the **infinitive**, remove **-er / -ir / -re**, and add the ending for the person. *jouer → jou → je joue*. The stem never changes for a regular verb, so once you know the six endings you know the whole verb.

tips.title: Nous is -ons and vous is -ez, almost always
tips.body: Across regular **-er** and **-re** verbs, and most irregulars, **nous** ends in **-ons** and **vous** in **-ez**. Only *être* (*nous sommes, vous êtes*), *faire* (*vous faites*) and *dire* (*vous dites*) break it. Learn those three exceptions and the plurals look after themselves.

tips.title: The -ir family keeps its -iss-
tips.body: *finir* → *nous fin**iss**ons, vous fin**iss**ez, ils fin**iss**ent*. The plural forms of regular **-ir** verbs all carry **-iss-**. Leaving it out is the commonest slip in this family.

tips.title: Four irregulars carry most of the language
tips.body: **Être, avoir, aller, faire** are irregular and appear in almost every sentence — *je suis, j'ai, je vais, je fais*. They cannot be worked out from a rule, so learn all six forms of each by heart before anything else.

tips.title: One French present does the work of two English ones
tips.body: *Je joue* is both *I play* and *I am playing*. French has no *am + -ing* tense, so never try to translate *am playing* with *suis* — *je joue* already means it. (*Je suis en train de jouer*, I am busy playing, exists for emphasis and is Higher only.)

why.matters: The present tense is where every other French tense starts. Most verbs end in *-er* and follow one pattern, so learning that pattern once covers most of the language; two smaller families follow theirs; and four irregular verbs, *être*, *avoir*, *aller* and *faire*, carry so much of French that they build the perfect tense, the near future and dozens of expressions. One French present also does the work of two English ones, *I play* and *I am playing*. Get the endings right here and the marks for accuracy follow you through every topic.

examples.title: One word where English needs two
examples.body: An English speaker writing about a Saturday reaches for *I am playing* and looks for a French *am*. There is none. *Je joue* is *I play*, *I am playing* and *I do play* all at once, and the time phrase does the rest: *maintenant* for now, *tous les jours* for a habit, *le samedi* for every Saturday. The trap runs the other way too: *je suis jouer* is the error the examiner sees most in Year 9, and it comes from translating the English word by word.

examples.title: Chop the ending, add the new one
examples.body: Take any *-er* verb, cut off the *-er*, and the stem stays put while six endings move: *-e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent*. Four of the six sound identical, *joue, joues, joue, jouent*, so the spelling is where the marks are, and the *ils* form's silent *-ent* is the one the dictation loves. Once the stem-and-ending picture is in your head, a new verb is a matter of one cut, and the same picture will serve for every tense that follows.

examples.title: Four verbs that carry the language
examples.body: *Être, avoir, aller* and *faire* refuse the pattern, and they are worth the effort because they are everywhere: *j'ai quinze ans* is *avoir*, *je vais sortir* is *aller* building the near future, *j'ai joué* is *avoir* building the perfect, *il fait beau* is *faire* doing the weather. Learn the four sets of six forms as sounds you can say in your sleep and a large part of GCSE French unlocks at once.

steps.title: Regular -er verbs
steps.body:
Most French verbs end in **-er**, and almost all of them follow one pattern (*aller* is the big exception). That makes it the most useful pattern in the language.

**The method**: take the infinitive, **remove -er** to find the stem, and **add the ending** for the person.

*jouer* → stem *jou* → *je jou**e**, tu jou**es**, il jou**e**, nous jou**ons**, vous jou**ez**, ils jou**ent***.

The endings are **-e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent**.

**Three things to notice.** The *je*, *tu*, *il* and *ils* forms all **sound the same** — *joue, joues, joue, jouent* — so spelling is where the marks are. Before a vowel, *je* becomes **j'**: *j'aime, j'habite*. And **on** takes the *il* form: *on joue*.

**Verbs that work like this**: *aimer, jouer, regarder, écouter, manger, habiter, parler, travailler, chanter, danser, porter*, and *acheter* with one accent change (*j'achète, ils achètent*). Hundreds more.

**What the present tense means.** *Je joue* covers **I play**, **I am playing** and **I do play**. French has one present tense for all three, so *am playing* is never translated with *suis*.

visuals.alt: A conjugation table for jouer in the present tense, showing the stem and ending for each person

visuals.fallback: Verbes en -er: jouer — to play; regarder — to watch; écouter — to listen to; manger — to eat; habiter — to live; parler — to speak; travailler — to work; chanter — to sing; danser — to dance; acheter — to buy; aimer — to like; porter — to wear, to carry

steps.title: Regular -ir and -re verbs
steps.body:
Two smaller families follow their own patterns. The method is the same — chop the ending, add the new one — but the endings differ.

**-ir verbs like finir**: *finir* → stem *fin* → *je fin**is**, tu fin**is**, il fin**it**, nous fin**issons**, vous fin**issez**, ils fin**issent***.

The endings are **-is, -is, -it, -issons, -issez, -issent**. The thing to hold on to is the **-iss-** in all three plural forms. *Choisir* (to choose) and *remplir* (to fill) work the same way.

**-re verbs like vendre**: *vendre* → stem *vend* → *je vend**s**, tu vend**s**, il vend, nous vend**ons**, vous vend**ez**, ils vend**ent***.

The endings are **-s, -s, (nothing), -ons, -ez, -ent**. The *il* form has **no ending at all** — just the stem. *Attendre* (to wait), *répondre* (to answer) and *perdre* (to lose) follow it.

**Not every -ir or -re verb follows these patterns.** *Partir* and *sortir* drop a consonant in the singular (*je pars, nous partons*), *venir* changes its stem (*je viens, nous venons, ils viennent*), *ouvrir* takes -er endings (*j'ouvre, nous ouvrons*), and *prendre* goes *je prends, nous prenons, ils prennent*. Learn those as they come; the tables here are for verbs like *finir* and *vendre*.

**Across the families**, notice what stays the same: **nous -ons** and **vous -ez** in -er and -re, and **ils -ent** in all three. Those shared endings are the ones to make automatic.

steps.title: The four big irregulars
steps.body:
Four verbs refuse to follow any pattern, and they are the four you use most. There is no shortcut: learn all six forms of each.

**Être — to be**: *je suis, tu es, il est, nous sommes, vous êtes, ils sont*.

**Avoir — to have**: *j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez, ils ont*.

**Aller — to go**: *je vais, tu vas, il va, nous allons, vous allez, ils vont*.

**Faire — to do, to make**: *je fais, tu fais, il fait, nous faisons, vous faites, ils font*.

**Why these four matter beyond themselves.** *Avoir* and *être* build the **perfect tense** later this term (*j'ai joué, je suis allé*). *Aller* builds the **near future** (*je vais jouer*). *Faire* appears in dozens of expressions — *faire du sport, faire les devoirs, il fait beau*. Knowing them cold unlocks three more tenses and a great deal of vocabulary.

**Watch the plural exceptions.** *Nous sommes* and *vous êtes* break the *-ons / -ez* rule, and *vous faites* has no *-ez*. *Ils sont, ils ont, ils vont, ils font* all end in **-ont** — a useful pattern within the irregularity.

steps.title: Using the present
steps.body: The present tense does three jobs, and the **time phrase** tells you which. **What is happening now**: *maintenant, en ce moment, aujourd'hui*. *En ce moment, je regarde un film.* **What you do regularly**: *tous les jours, le week-end, souvent, d'habitude, le samedi*. *Le samedi, je joue au foot.* Note *le samedi* means **on Saturdays** — every one — while *samedi* alone is one particular Saturday. **Facts that are always true**: *j'habite à Leeds, je suis anglais, mon frère a douze ans*. **Frequency words** lift a plain sentence. One-word adverbs usually go straight after the conjugated verb (*je joue souvent*, never *je souvent joue*); some, such as *souvent* and *quelquefois*, and longer phrases such as *de temps en temps* can also open the sentence. The words: *toujours* (always), *souvent* (often), *quelquefois* (sometimes), *de temps en temps* (from time to time), *rarement* (rarely), and *ne … jamais* (never). *Je ne regarde jamais la télé.* The **jamais** replaces *pas* and sits in the same place. **Negatives** wrap the conjugated verb: *je **ne** joue **pas**, il n'écoute **pas**, nous **ne** finissons **pas***. *Ne* becomes *n'* before a vowel.

visuals.fallback: Quand et à quelle fréquence: maintenant — now; en ce moment — at the moment; aujourd'hui — today; tous les jours — every day; le week-end — at the weekend; le samedi — on Saturdays; toujours — always; souvent — often; quelquefois — sometimes; de temps en temps — from time to time; rarement — rarely; ne … jamais — never; d'habitude — usually

check.solution: **On Saturdays** — every Saturday. *Samedi* on its own, with no article, means one particular Saturday: this one, next or last, depending on the tense.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Name the family before you conjugate.** Every error in the present starts with the wrong endings on the right stem. *-er*, *-ir* like *finir*, *-re* like *vendre*, or irregular (*partir, venir, ouvrir* and *prendre* have their own patterns) — decide, then apply.

**Keep the -iss-.** *Nous finissons, vous choisissez, ils remplissent.* The regular -ir plurals all carry it, and dropping it is the family's signature mistake.

**Leave the -re il form bare.** *Il attend, elle vend, on répond.* No ending. Adding *-t* or *-e* by analogy with the other families is common and wrong.

**Learn the big four in full, and know why.** *Être* and *avoir* are the perfect tense's helpers; *aller* is the near future; *faire* is in a hundred expressions. Time spent on their six forms each is repaid in three later tenses.

**Never translate the English continuous.** *I am playing* is *je joue*. *Je suis jouer* is not French. The single present covers *play, am playing* and *do play*.

**Distinguish le samedi from samedi.** With the article it is habitual — *on Saturdays*. Without, it is one particular Saturday. The same holds for every day of the week.

**Place jamais where pas goes.** *Je ne regarde **jamais** la télé.* *Jamais* replaces *pas*; it does not join it. *Ne … pas jamais* is an error.

**Vary the subject.** A piece of writing entirely in *je* reads flat. *Mes amis jouent, ma sœur chante, on mange ensemble* — plural and third-person forms show you control the whole table, which is what accuracy across persons means to an examiner.

**Mind the spelling changes.** *Nous mangeons* keeps the **e**, *nous commençons* takes a **cedilla**, both to keep the sound soft. These are regular verbs with one spelling rule attached.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Method: **remove the ending, add the new one**; the stem stays.
- **-er**: -e, -es, -e, -ons, -ez, -ent.
- **-ir** (like *finir*): -is, -is, -it, -issons, -issez, -issent — keep the **-iss-**.
- **-re** (like *vendre*): -s, -s, **nothing**, -ons, -ez, -ent.
- **Nous -ons** and **vous -ez** almost everywhere; **ils -ent**.
- *Je* → **j'** before a vowel; **on** takes the *il* form.
- **Être**: suis, es, est, sommes, êtes, sont.
- **Avoir**: ai, as, a, avons, avez, ont.
- **Aller**: vais, vas, va, allons, allez, vont.
- **Faire**: fais, fais, fait, faisons, faites, font.
- The big four build the **perfect**, the **near future**, and many expressions.
- One present = *I play*, *I am playing*, *I do play*.
- Time phrases choose the meaning: *maintenant*, *tous les jours*, *le samedi*.
- Negatives: **ne … pas** round the verb; **ne … jamais** for never.
- *Nous mangeons* keeps the **e**; *nous commençons* takes a **ç**.

questions.solution: **Il n'écoute pas de musique.** *Ne* becomes *n'* before the vowel, and *pas* follows the verb. After *ne … pas*, *de la* becomes *de*.

options: Je ne joue pas jamais au tennis.
Je ne joue jamais au tennis.
Je ne jamais joue au tennis.
questions.solution: **Je ne joue jamais au tennis.** *Jamais* replaces *pas* and sits after the verb; *ne* is still needed.

questions.prompt: A student writes "*Je suis jouer au foot*" for "I am playing football". What is the error?
options: Jouer should become jouant after the verb suis
There is no continuous form: it should be je joue
It should be je suis en jouer au foot
Only the article au is wrong in the sentence
questions.solution: The French **present** already means *am playing*: **je joue au foot**. *Suis* + infinitive is an English structure that does not exist in French.

questions.prompt: Translate into English: **le dimanche, on mange ensemble et mes parents ne travaillent jamais**.
options: This Sunday, we eat together and my parents never work.
On Sundays, we eat together and my parents always work.
On Sundays, we ate together and my parents never worked.
On Sundays, we eat together and my parents never work.
questions.solution: **On Sundays, we eat together and my parents never work.** *Le dimanche* is habitual; *on* is *we*; *ne … jamais* is never. *This Sunday* misses that *le* + a day means every week; *always work* reads *jamais* as its opposite; and *ate … worked* puts two present-tense verbs into the past.

questions.prompt: Why is **nous mangeons** spelt with an **e** before **-ons**?
options: Because nous forms always add an e
To keep the g soft before o
It is a spelling mistake that has become standard
questions.solution: Without the **e**, *mangons* would have a hard *g*. The **e** keeps the soft sound of the infinitive, just as **ç** does in *nous commençons*. *Manger* is otherwise entirely regular.

Mes parents travaillent beaucoup pendant la semaine, mais ils ne travaillent jamais le dimanche. Ma sœur choisit toujours la musique dans la voiture. Je ne regarde jamais la télé le matin. questions.prompt: Which set of endings belongs to regular **-re** verbs?
questions.solution: **-s, -s, (nothing), -ons, -ez, -ent.** The *il* form is bare. *-e, -es, -e…* is the -er set, *-is, -is, -it, -issons…* is the -ir set, and *-s, -s, -t, …, -ont* mixes in the irregular *-ont*.

questions.prompt: Translate into French: **from time to time, my friends and I go to the cinema**. (Use on.)
questions.solution: **De temps en temps, on va au cinéma avec mes amis.** *On* takes the *il* form — *va* — and *au* is *à + le*.

examTechnique.body:
**Identify the family first** — -er, -ir like *finir*, -re like *vendre*, or irregular — then chop and add. Keep the **-iss-** in -ir plurals and leave the -re *il* form **bare**.

Learn **être, avoir, aller, faire** in full. Never write *suis* + infinitive for *am doing*; the present already means it. Put **jamais** where *pas* goes.
examinerErrors: Adding an ending to the il form of an -re verb.
Translating "am playing" as je suis jouer.
Forgetting the e in nous mangeons.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the family before conjugating and gets every ending right across **several persons**, not only *je*. It keeps the **-iss-**, leaves the -re *il* form bare, and has the **four irregulars** cold — including *vous faites* and *vous êtes*. It never reaches for *suis* to say *am doing*, places **jamais** correctly, and knows *le samedi* is habitual. It adds **frequency phrases** for free detail and handles the spelling changes in *mangeons* and *commençons* without hesitation.
